title: Clauses, Conditionals, and Critical Reading
subject: inggris
summary: Present perfect, relative clauses, second conditional, gerunds, expository texts, reliable sources, and logical fallacies.
objectives: use relative pronouns who, which, where, and whose
use the second conditional for imaginary situations
use gerunds after verbs like enjoy and avoid
find the main idea and the role of linking words in an expository text
judge sources and spot common fallacies

sections.title: Relative clauses
sections.html: who for people, which for things, where for places, whose for possession. "The scientist who discovered the vaccine received an award."

sections.title: If I were ...
sections.html:
Second conditionalIf + past simple (were for all subjects), would + verb

If I were a bird, I would fly over the sea. It talks about something unreal or unlikely.

sections.title: Gerunds
sections.html: After enjoy, avoid, finish, and mind, use verb + -ing: She enjoys reading novels.

sections.title: Reading an expository text
sections.html: Find the main idea by asking what most sentences are about. Linking words show how ideas connect: however (contrast), moreover (addition), for example (example), therefore (result). In a text about mangroves, "However" turns from their benefits to the threats they face.

sections.title: Sources and fallacies
sections.html:
A reliable source explains its methods, can be checked, and does not profit from the conclusion. Watch out for common fallacies:

  • Bandwagon: "Everyone does it, so it must be fine."
  • Anecdote: "My friend got sick, so the vaccine does not work."
  • Correlation as cause: two things rising together do not prove one causes the other.
